newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Second Earth Summit opens with call for action.
newsitem.headline: Second Earth Summit opens with call for action.

text.p: The second environmental "Earth Summit" opened on Monday with a dire warning from its chairman that the world could soon pass "the point of no return" if it continued to destroy the planet.

"We as a species, as a planet, are teetering on the edge, living unsustainably and perpetuating inequity, and may soon pass the point of no return," said Razali Ismail of Malaysia, president of the United Nations General Assembly.
Leaders and envoys from 173 countries are meeting in New York for the "Earth Summit Plus 5" to deliver a report on how they have followed through on the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro.
But Razali issued a crushing condemnation of their efforts:

"Those at Rio who made serious commitments have not followed through on their promises," he said. Instead they resorted to "spinning, declarations of intent, pointing the finger at others and pandering to interest groups."
In Rio some 10,000 diplomats produced "Agenda 21" laying down 2,500 goals. These were followed in the years since then by treaties on climate change, conservation and desertification.
But early speakers at the summit said the environment had in fact deteriorated in the last five years.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan told delegates that "at stake this week is the capacity of the international system of states to act decisively in the global interest."
He said that "failure to act now could damage our planet irreversibly, unleashing a spiral of increased hunger, deprivation, disease and squalor."
"We must not fail," he said.
The delegates were welcomed by U.S. Vice President Al Gore who said action needed to be taken on global warming, forests and poverty.

"Sustainable development requires sustained commitment, Gore said. "We must roll up our sleeves and go to work. These are not small tasks. We must make sustainable development a guiding principle of the 21st century."

But Gore went no further than current U.S. policy, criticised by Europeans for not setting goals to reduce greenhouse gases that cause global warming and by the Third world for reducing funds they need to develop environmentally-safe economic growth.
Britain, Germany and France have already criticised Washington for not agreeing to European targets for emission cuts -- a 15 percent reduction by the year 2010 -- of the greenhouse gases.
President Bill Clinton resisted European pressure for specific targets at the Group of Seven summit in Denver that ended on Sunday.

The United States accounts for nearly 23 percent of all greenhouse gases emitted around the world when fossil fuels like oil and coal are burned. Scientists say these emissions will lead to dangerous climate changes in the next century.

In second place is China with 13.3 percent, followed by Russia with 7.2 percent, Japan with 5 percent and Germany with 3.8 percent. The emissions are declining in Russia and Germany but rising in the United States, Japan and China.
No issue promises to be more divisive at the summit than pledges in Rio to help poor nations develop without repeating the pollution catastrophes of industrial countries.
Most rich countries agreed in principle to increase foreign aid to 0.7 percent of their gross national product but few did so.
Instead aid has declined steadily since 1992 from 0.35 percent to 0.27 percent in 1995.
According to the Organisation of Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), only the Netherlands, Denmark, Norway and Sweden topped the 0.7 percent goal.

In absolute terms, Japan in 1995 led development assistance with $14.4 billion followed by France with $8.4 billion, Germany with $7.5 billion. The United States, is in fifth place. Its total aid fell to $7.3 billion in 1995 compared to $9.9 billion the previous year.
